newsitem.title: USA: Medicine moratorium can reduce drug resistance.
newsitem.headline: Medicine moratorium can reduce drug resistance.

text.p: Overuse of antibiotics has encouraged drug-resistant bacteria to thrive, but a new study shows a moratorium on use can restore the effectiveness of a drug.

Researchers in Finland looked at the drug erythromycin. Early in the 1990s, when the number of cases resistant to the antibiotic was quickly rising, Finland instituted a nationwide push to stop prescribing it and switch to alternative drugs.

Dr. Helena Seppala of the National Public Health Institute in Finland reports in Thursday's edition of the New England Journal of Medicine that consumption of the drug was nearly cut in half within a year.
And, four years later, the rate of resistance among streptococcal bacteria had dropped from 16.5 percent in 1992 to 8.6 percent in 1996.
"Our data confirm that the level of antimicrobial resistance in the community can be reduced by decreasing the use of antibiotics," said Seppala and her colleagues in the Journal.

"This is an impressive example of how an enlightened national policy on antibiotic use can become an effective public health measure," said Dr. Morton Swartz of Massachusetts General Hospital in an editorial in the Journal.

A 1996 survey by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found that doctors admitted that they could probably reduce their number of antibiotic prescriptions by 20 to 50 percent without harming any patients.
CDC epidemiologist Benjamin Schwartz has estimated that about a third of the 50 million antibiotic prescriptions given out each year are unnecessary.

"When they are imprudently prescribed for nonspecific symptoms or infection that is probably viral, their use may only contribute to bacterial resistance...in hospitals, in the community, and in animal feedlots," Schwartz said.
